Diamond. Pure carbon crystallised under extreme pressure and temperature deep within the Earth's mantle. It's the hardest naturally occurring mineral and the most prized gemstone, valued for its transparency, refractive index, and durability. Diamonds are brought to the surface via rare kimberlite and lamproite pipes during explosive volcanic eruptions.

Diamond is pure carbon arranged in an isometric crystal lattice, with each atom bonded to four others in an extremely strong three-dimensional network. It's rated ten on the Mohs hardness scale—the hardest natural mineral. No natural substance can scratch it except another diamond, and it's abrasive enough to cut all others. Diamond forms only at pressures exceeding five gigapascals and temperatures above twelve hundred degrees Celsius, conditions found in the mantle more than a hundred and fifty kilometres below the surface.

The refractive index of diamond is exceptionally high, about two point four two, which gives diamonds their characteristic brilliance and "fire"—the spectral dispersion. However, diamond is metastable at Earth's surface. Over an incredibly long period of time, it would revert to graphite, but the activation energy required is so high that diamonds persist indefinitely. Kimberlite pipes are narrow vertical magma channels that tap the upper mantle and erupt with violent force, bringing diamonds to the surface. Industrial diamonds are used as abrasives, cutting tools, and heat sinks. Gem-grade diamonds command high prices based on the "Four Cs": carat, colour, clarity, and cut.

Diamond is an allotrope of carbon, as is graphite, but the crystal structure makes them vastly different. Diamond competes with corundum as one of the hardest common minerals, though diamond wins and corundum is far more abundant. Diamonds define the top end of the Mohs hardness scale. Kimberlite is an ultramafic igneous rock that transports diamonds from the mantle. And diamonds remain the most valued gemstones by economic value overall, though that value varies by colour and clarity.
